SEMICONDUCTOR CHIP MASK WORK PROTECTION (17 U.S.C. §§ 901-914) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Semiconductor, Inc.

DECLARATION
This information sheet describes the federal Semiconductor Chip Protection Act of 1984, codified at 17 U.S.C. §§ 901-914 (chapter 9 of the Copyright Act) -- a distinct, sui generis intellectual property right that protects the topography of a semiconductor chip's layered circuitry design, called a "mask work," separately from copyright, patent, or trade secret law. It is prepared with reference to A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015., associated with Acme Semiconductor, Inc. This sheet describes the statutory definitions of "mask work" and "semiconductor chip product" in § 901, the eligibility and non-originality/idea-exclusion limits on protection in § 902, ownership and transfer under § 903, the 10-year term in § 904, the exclusive rights in § 905, the reverse-engineering limitation in § 906, the 2-year registration deadline in § 908, the optional notice form in § 909, and the preemption of equivalent state-law protection in § 912; it does not evaluate whether A bronze sculpture titled ‘Pacific Light,’ installed in the plaza in 2015. qualifies for mask work protection, does not prepare or file any application with the Register of Copyrights, and does not calculate any specific term, registration deadline, or infringement remedy. This document is distinct from the corpus's existing Copyright Assignment, Patent Assignment, Patent License, Trademark License, Software License, and trade-secret documents -- mask work protection is a separate statutory scheme from all of them, sharing an administering office (the Register of Copyrights) with copyright but not copyright's own subject-matter or duration rules. This sheet is educational only; it is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney, and it does not itself request, register, or enforce protection for any mask work.

WHAT COUNTS AS A "MASK WORK" AND A "SEMICONDUCTOR CHIP PRODUCT"
The statute defines two closely related terms. A "semiconductor chip product" is the final or intermediate form of any product having two or more layers of metallic, insulating, or semiconductor material placed on, or etched away from, a piece of semiconductor material in a predetermined pattern, and intended to perform electronic circuitry functions. A "mask work" is the layered design itself: a series of related images, however fixed or encoded, that represent the predetermined, three-dimensional pattern of material present or removed from the layers of a semiconductor chip product, where each image in the series corresponds to the pattern of one layer of the chip product. In short, the semiconductor chip product is the physical object; the mask work is the layout pattern embodied in it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — 17 U.S.C. § 901(a)(1) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, definition of "semiconductor chip product" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/901)
  "a “mask work” is a series of related images, however fixed or encoded— (A) having or representing the predetermined, three-dimensional pattern of metallic, insulating, or semiconductor material present or removed from the layers of a semiconductor chip product; and (B) in which series the relation of the images to one another is that each image has the pattern of the surface of one form of the semiconductor chip product;"
  — 17 U.S.C. § 901(a)(2) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, definition of "mask work" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/901)

Both quotations below come from the same statutory subsection, § 901(a), so they are treated as one source consulted once, not as two independent sources. This is a federal statute of nationwide application, not California-specific law. WHAT THE STATUTE DOES NOT PROTECT: NON-ORIGINAL AND STAPLE DESIGNS, AND IDEAS
Protection under the statute is not automatic for every chip layout. It is unavailable for a mask work that is not original, and separately unavailable for a mask work that consists of designs that are staple, commonplace, or familiar in the semiconductor industry -- or variations of such designs -- combined in a way that, considered as a whole, is not itself original. The statute also draws an idea/expression-style line similar to copyright's: in no case does protection extend to any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept, principle, or discovery, regardless of the form in which it is described, explained, illustrated, or embodied in the mask work.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Protection under this chapter shall not be available for a mask work that— (1) is not original; or (2) consists of designs that are staple, commonplace, or familiar in the semiconductor industry, or variations of such designs, combined in a way that, considered as a whole, is not original."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 902(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, non-original and staple-design exclusion (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/902)
  "In no case does protection under this chapter for a mask work extend to any idea, procedure, process, system, method of operation, concept, principle, or discovery, regardless of the form in which it is described, explained, illustrated, or embodied in such work."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 902(c) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, idea/procedure/process exclusion (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/902)

Neither subsection is defined further by the statute -- the statute does not itself explain what makes a combination of staple or commonplace elements "original" as a whole, and this clause does not evaluate whether the specific mask work described in this document meets or fails either exclusion. Section 902(a)'s separate nationality/treaty eligibility requirements (protection generally requires the owner to be a U.S. national or domiciliary, a national of a treaty country, a stateless person, or for the work to be first commercially exploited in the United States) are not addressed in this clause. This is a federal statute of nationwide application. OWNERSHIP AND TRANSFER OF MASK WORK RIGHTS
The exclusive rights in a mask work subject to protection belong to the owner of the mask work. The owner may transfer all of those rights, or license all or less than all of them, by any written instrument signed by the owner or the owner's duly authorized agent; the statute also allows the rights to be transferred or licensed by operation of law, bequeathed by will, or to pass as personal property under the applicable laws of intestate succession.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  "The owner of the exclusive rights in a mask work may transfer all of those rights, or license all or less than all of those rights, by any written instrument signed by such owner or a duly authorized agent of the owner."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 903(b) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, transfer and licensing (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/903)

DURATION: TEN YEARS FROM REGISTRATION OR FIRST COMMERCIAL EXPLOITATION
Protection commences on the date the mask work is registered with the Register of Copyrights under § 908, or the date it is first commercially exploited anywhere in the world, whichever occurs first. Protection then lasts ten years from that commencement date, and every term of protection under the statute runs to the end of the calendar year in which it would otherwise expire. The date recorded for this document as the mask work's first commercial exploitation, if any, is March 1, 2026, or leave blank if not yet commercially exploited.

THE OWNER'S EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS
The owner of a protected mask work has the exclusive rights to do, and to authorize, three things: to reproduce the mask work by optical, electronic, or any other means; to import or distribute a semiconductor chip product in which the mask work is embodied; and to induce or knowingly cause another person to do either of those acts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The owner of a mask work provided protection under this chapter has the exclusive rights to do and to authorize any of the following: (1) to reproduce the mask work by optical, electronic, or any other means; (2) to import or distribute a semiconductor chip product in which the mask work is embodied; and (3) to induce or knowingly to cause another person to do any of the acts described in paragraphs (1) and (2)."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 905 (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, exclusive rights in mask works (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/905)

This is a federal statute of nationwide application. THE REVERSE-ENGINEERING LIMITATION
The exclusive rights described above are subject to a built-in reverse-engineering limitation. It is not an infringement for a person to reproduce a mask work solely to teach, analyze, or evaluate the concepts or techniques embodied in the mask work, or the circuitry, logic flow, or organization of components it uses, and it is likewise not an infringement for a person who performs that analysis or evaluation to incorporate the results in an original mask work that is made to be distributed. A separate provision of the same section allows the owner of a particular lawfully made semiconductor chip product to import, distribute, or otherwise dispose of or use -- but not reproduce -- that particular chip product without the mask work owner's authority.

  — 17 U.S.C. § 906(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, reverse-engineering limitation (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/906)

THE TWO-YEAR REGISTRATION DEADLINE
Unlike copyright, which now exists automatically on fixation, mask work protection carries a hard registration deadline tied to commercial use. The mask work owner may apply to the Register of Copyrights for registration of a claim of protection, and protection under the statute terminates if that application is not made within two years after the date the mask work is first commercially exploited anywhere in the world.

OPTIONAL MASK WORK NOTICE
The statute permits, but does not require, an owner to affix a notice to a protected mask work and to masks and semiconductor chip products embodying it. Affixing the notice is not itself a condition of protection, but it does constitute prima facie evidence of notice of protection -- a fact relevant to the statute's separate innocent-purchaser limitation on remedies. The notice consists of the words "mask work," the symbol *M*, or the symbol Ⓜ (the letter M in a circle), together with the name of the mask work's owner or an abbreviation by which that name is recognized or generally known.

PREEMPTION OF EQUIVALENT STATE-LAW PROTECTION
This federal scheme displaces overlapping state law. The statute preempts the laws of any state to the extent those laws provide rights or remedies with respect to a mask work that are equivalent to the rights or remedies the federal statute itself provides, though the statute limits that preemption to actions filed on or after January 1, 1986.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The provisions of this chapter shall preempt the laws of any State to the extent those laws provide any rights or remedies with respect to a mask work which are equivalent to those rights or remedies provided by this chapter, except that such preemption shall be effective only with respect to actions filed on or after January 1, 1986."
  — 17 U.S.C. § 912(c) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Semiconductor Chip Protection Act, preemption of equivalent state law (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/17/912)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only 17 U.S.C. § 912(c); it does not address § 912(a)'s separate rule that nothing in this chapter affects rights or remedies available under copyright (chapters 1-8 or 10 of title 17) or patent law (title 35), § 912(b)'s cross-reference rule, or § 912(d)'s saving clause for rights concerning a mask work first commercially exploited before July 1, 1983, none of which are quoted here. This clause states only that the federal statute preempts equivalent state-law rights and remedies concerning mask works specifically -- it does not state, and should not be read to suggest, that California trade secret law (which protects the confidentiality of an unpublished chip design or manufacturing process, not a mask work already embodied in a distributed product) is preempted by this statute; trade secret protection and mask work protection address different subject matter and can both apply to different aspects of the same underlying chip design at different points in its development. This is a federal statute of nationwide application; this clause does not evaluate whether any specific California statute or common-law doctrine would in fact provide a "right or remedy" "equivalent" to this chapter's own rights and remedies.
